title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Kosovo sits within the Balkan biodiversity hotspot, one of the most species-rich regions in Europe. Evidence-based conservation — designating protected areas, screening development proposals, and reporting against the EU Nature Directives — depends on knowing which species occur where.
The Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) aggregates species occurrence records published by museums, research institutions, monitoring programmes and citizen-science platforms worldwide. This report brings the GBIF holdings for the territory of Kosovo into a single, quality-controlled, openly downloadable evidence base, and highlights the records that relate to species protected under the EU Birds and Habitats Directives or assessed as threatened on the IUCN Red List — and to the invasive alien species the EU regulates as a threat to all of them.


46,831Quality-checked records


4,096Species recorded


5,073Directive-listed records


37IUCN-threatened species


5EU invasive species recorded


38 / 38Municipalities with records

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Data provenance and citation
The occurrence data were obtained through the GBIF asynchronous download service, which mints a permanent Digital Object Identifier (DOI) for the exact extract used here. Citing that DOI allows any reader to retrieve the identical dataset, and passes credit back to the institutions that published the records.

Dataset DOI: https://doi.org/10.15468/dl.wzpexq GBIF download key: 0003504-260903145123482 Retrieved: 28 September 2026 Spatial filter: GADM boundary XKO (Kosovo) Contributing datasets: 125, from 80 publishing institutions Suggested citation GBIF Occurrence Download https://doi.org/10.15468/dl.wzpexq Accessed from R via rgbif (https://github.com/ropensci/rgbif) on 2026-09-05

Two reference layers are used alongside the occurrence records, and both are cited here because conclusions drawn from an overlay depend on the layer as much as on the points. Administrative boundaries — the national outline and the 38 municipalities alike — are OpenStreetMap, for the reasons set out under A note on the spatial filter below. Protected areas are the European Environment Agency’s inventory of Nationally designated areas, version 24 (July 2026).

Administrative boundaries: OpenStreetMap — national outline and 38 municipalities Licence: Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0, © OpenStreetMap contributorsSource: openstreetmap.org/copyright Protected areas: EEA Nationally designated areas (NatDA/CDDA), v24 (July 2026) DOI: https://doi.org/10.2909/028003e7-7585-4d69-92fc-7f81e0cc2340 Licence: CC-BY 4.0, © European Environment Agency Coverage for Kosovo: 237 designated sites, 48 with a mapped boundary







NoteA note on the spatial filter





Records were selected using the GADM administrative boundary for Kosovo (GID XKO) rather than the ISO country code XK. The GADM boundary is a true spatial filter, so it also captures records whose publisher left the country field blank or assigned it to a neighbouring state — a common situation for cross-border survey data. Queried against the GBIF occurrence API without any further filters at the time of extraction, gadmGid=XKO returned 52,290 records against 48,947 for country=XK, about 7 per cent more.
Note that the GADM identifier for Kosovo is XKO. The similar-looking code XKX is the World Bank / ISO alpha-3 style code and is not recognised by GADM — pred("gadm", "XKX") returns zero records rather than an error, so a pipeline using it would silently produce an empty dataset.
Selecting the records is not the same as defining the country. GADM’s Kosovo polygon is a generalisation: 1,210 vertices for a border that runs 743 km, roughly one point every 600 m of a line that turns far more often than that. Sampling both candidate borders every 200 m and measuring to Eurostat’s GISCO 1:1M line — an independent official digitisation of the same international border — GADM’s sits a median 587 m from it, and 2,980 m at the ninetieth percentile. OpenStreetMap’s sits 60 m and 189 m; the residual there is GISCO’s own generalisation rather than OSM’s. The areas tell the same story: published figures for Kosovo cluster between 10,887 km² (World Bank) and 10,910 km², and OpenStreetMap’s polygon measures 10,898 km², inside that range, where GADM’s measures 10,828 km², below all of it. The two outlines disagree over 755 km², 6.9 per cent of the country, and run up to 4.1 km apart.
This report therefore selects on GADM, because that is the filter GBIF offers, and screens and draws on OpenStreetMap, because that is where the border actually is. Both errors in GADM’s outline matter, and only one of them can be repaired here:

Where GADM bulges outward, it swept in 1,776 records that are not in Kosovo. Their own publishers say as much: 1,030 are stamped ME, 320 MK, 284 RS and 45 AL, against 97 stamped XK. The country-coordinate test removes them — see below.
Where GADM falls short, 412 km² of Kosovo lies outside the polygon GBIF filtered on, and records there were never in the download to begin with. Nothing downstream can recover them. Closing that gap means selecting on a geometry predicate instead, which mints a new download and a new DOI.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Summary statistics
Each row below is a distinct thematic extract of the cleaned dataset. All seven are available for download at the end of this report.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Data quality control
Aggregated occurrence data carries well-known geographic artefacts: records placed at the centre of a country, at a museum’s own address, or at coordinates of exactly zero. Every record was screened with CoordinateCleaner and only records passing all tests were retained.
The screening finds nothing to remove, and that is the expected result rather than a broken test. GBIF’s own filters excluded records without coordinates and records it had already flagged with a geospatial issue before the extract was built, and the extract was selected by a true spatial filter, so the failure modes these tests look for have no way into the dataset. The screening is kept because it is the guarantee: it would catch them if they ever appeared.












NoteWhich tests were applied, which were left out, and the polygon they all depend on





Applied: zero coordinates, country-coordinate mismatch, GBIF headquarters, known biodiversity institutions, and identical latitude/longitude values.
Deliberately not applied: the capital city and country centroid tests. Both discard records falling within a fixed radius of a capital or of a country’s geometric centre. Kosovo is small enough that Pristina and the national centroid both sit well inside the territory, so these tests would remove a large number of entirely legitimate records — including most urban biodiversity data. They can be enabled in pipeline.R by setting use_capitals_test = TRUE.
The country-coordinate test needed two corrections, and both fail silently.
It cannot see Kosovo by default. Natural Earth, the reference dataset CoordinateCleaner ships with, records Kosovo with no assigned ISO alpha-3 code. Run against that default the test flags 100 per cent of Kosovo records as mismatches and, with value = "clean", returns an empty data frame without warning. The pipeline therefore supplies a bespoke reference polygon stamped with the code used in the occurrence data.
That polygon then has to be the right one. Built from Natural Earth’s 1:50m outline — 72 vertices for the whole country, straying up to 4.7 km from the true border — the test flagged 1,296 records on the strength of the outline’s own error. Built from GADM level 0, the polygon GBIF filters on, it flagged nothing at all, which looks like a clean bill of health and is in fact the test grading its own paper: every record lies inside that polygon by construction, so asking whether it does can only ever return yes.
The reference is now the OpenStreetMap outline, which is neither the coarse polygon nor the selecting one, and the test does what it is for. It flags 1,776 records, 3.7 per cent of those with coordinates. These are not borderline calls made by a wobbly line: 94 per cent of them carry a publisher-assigned country code of ME, MK, RS or AL, and they sit a median 552 m and up to 3.3 km beyond the border. They are the records GADM’s outward bulges swept into the download, and removing them is the point of the exercise.
The correction is not free. 235 species leave the dataset with them, having been recorded nowhere else in the extract. Most probably do occur in Kosovo — they were found a few hundred metres the wrong side of a line — but this extract no longer claims evidence that they do, which is the honest position for it to take.
Records within a set distance of the border can be kept instead by setting country_buffer in pipeline.R; it is NULL here, meaning a strict test.




How precisely are the records placed?
Passing the coordinate tests means a record is not obviously wrong. It does not mean the record is precise enough for every purpose. A great many Kosovo records come from atlas-style surveys that report to a 10 km square, and the stated coordinate uncertainty is the honest way to tell those apart from a GPS-located field observation.












NoteWhy coarse records are kept rather than filtered out





The GBIF Viewer developed for Ukraine discards records whose stated uncertainty exceeds a threshold, on the reasonable grounds that a record placed to the nearest 10 km cannot support a decision about a particular field.
Applied here with a 1 km threshold, that rule would remove 20 per cent of the records. If records that state no uncertainty at all were dropped as well, since they cannot show that they are precise, it would remove 89 per cent. 18 per cent carry an uncertainty of exactly 7,071 m, which is the half-diagonal of a 10 km square: these are atlas records, and they are perfectly good evidence that a species occurs in a landscape even though they say nothing about where in it. Discarding them would make the country look emptier than it is, which is the more dangerous error for conservation planning.
The pipeline therefore reports the precision profile, keeps coordinateUncertaintyInMeters in every export, and offers precision as a filter in the record explorer below. The threshold is available as coord_uncertainty_max in pipeline.R for anyone who does want it applied. Which precision is enough depends on the decision; the Natura 2000 questions page sets out three tiers, from national screening to the Standard Data Form.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Where the records are
Each map carries the same set of switchable layers, reached through the control in the top-right corner:

Occurrence records — individual records, clustered until you zoom in, each with a pop-up carrying the determination, the place, the stated accuracy and a link through to the record on GBIF, where the evidence and any photographs can be checked. Where a tab holds more than 10,000 records this layer is left off altogether rather than thinned to a sample, because a thinned layer of dots looks exactly like a thin one; the two density layers below then carry the same records, and the explorer further down maps them one at a time.
Record density — every record aggregated onto a 2 km grid and classed against a legend. This is the layer to read when the question is how many.
Heat map — the same information as a smooth surface, better for seeing the shape of the sampled and unsampled areas.
Protected areas — the nationally designated sites, shown as a green wash under the records so that whether a record falls inside one can be read at a glance. Hovering names the site, its designation, its size and how much has been recorded there. Two further layers sit alongside it in the control: the strict protection zones inside the larger sites, and the 189 natural monuments — veteran trees, springs and caves — that the register records as a point rather than a boundary.
Municipalities — administrative boundaries, with each unit’s own record and species count on hover.

The toolbar on the left adds full-screen, a distance and area measure, a polygon and rectangle sketching tool, and a place search, so an area of interest can be outlined and sized directly on the map.

All biodiversityBirdsBirds Directive, Annex IHabitats DirectiveHabitats Directive, Annex IIIUCN threatenedInvasive alien species



























































Both density layers are the more informative reading of survey effort. Dense cells frequently mark well-visited sites rather than exceptionally rich ones, and pale areas usually indicate that nobody has yet surveyed there. Both readings matter when prioritising future fieldwork.






NoteHow the density layers are built, and why the heat map changed





Occurrence counts are extraordinarily uneven. Rounded to about 110 m, Kosovo has 5,590 occupied positions; three quarters of them hold a single record, and the busiest holds more than thirteen thousand. Any display that treats that range naively collapses.
The heat map previously did exactly that. Leaflet’s heat layer draws each point at an opacity of intensity / max and then colours the accumulated opacity through a gradient, so feeding it raw counts made every occupied cell saturate identically. Two further defaults compounded it: a minimum-opacity floor that lifted empty-ish areas up to the same value as real clusters, and an internal zoom scaling that divides every intensity by 2^(maxZoom - currentZoom) — about a thousandfold at the country view — pushing the whole surface onto that floor. The result was a single flat wash.
The layer now: aggregates onto the 110 m grid; maps the counts onto 0–1 with a logarithmic transform followed by a power below one, which spreads the crowded bottom of the distribution across usable values; pins the zoom reference so the surface means the same thing at every scale; and uses GBIF’s own density ramp, the one the occurrence map on gbif.org draws with. It runs yellow to red rather than through a single hue, but it darkens at every step, so “more” still reads as “darker” rather than as “a different colour” — which is the property a rainbow lacks and the reason one is not used here.
The Record density grid is the same information without the smoothing: 2 km cells, classed on roughly logarithmic breaks, with a legend and the exact count on hover. Use the heat map to see the shape of the coverage and the grid when a number is needed.









NoteAbout the common names shown in the pop-ups





Common names are not part of the GBIF download and are retrieved separately from the GBIF species API, which returns every name any publisher has supplied. The pipeline takes the most frequently published English name for each taxon, which recovers the standard name in the large majority of cases.
Publishers do, however, mis-tag the language of their names fairly often — roughly a fifth of the names returned as English for this dataset were in fact Norwegian, German, French, Swedish, Hungarian or Ukrainian. Names written in non-Latin scripts are filtered out automatically, but a mis-tagged Latin-script name occasionally survives. The scientific name is always the authoritative identifier; treat the common name as a convenience only.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Survey coverage by municipality
The map above answers “where are the records”. This one answers the question a planning authority actually asks: how well is my municipality covered? Records are counted per unit of area, because a large municipality with a moderate number of records may be far less well known than a small one with fewer.


















WarningOne municipality dominates the totals — read it carefully





Graçanicë / Gračanica holds far more records per square kilometre than anywhere else in the country. That is not a statement about its biodiversity. A single coordinate inside it carries more than thirteen thousand records, almost all of them bird observations submitted to one citizen-science platform from what is in practice one regularly watched site.
This is the characteristic shape of aggregated occurrence data and the reason raw record counts should never be read as species richness. The species column in the table above is the more honest comparison, and the two rank very differently: Graçanicë leads on records and sits well down the table on species.
That coordinate also shows why the municipal layer had to be replaced along with the national outline. It sits in the countryside south of Prishtina, on ground that belonged to Fushë Kosovë until the 2010 decentralisation moved it into the newly created municipality of Graçanicë. GADM 4.1 still draws the pre-2010 map, so every one of those thirteen thousand records used to be attributed to Fushë Kosovë — the wrong municipality, and the one a reader would have gone looking in.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Protected areas
A record’s value to conservation depends partly on where it falls. A population inside a national park is already covered by a management regime and a competent authority; the same population on undesignated ground is not. This section lays the occurrence data over Kosovo’s protected-area network and reports what each contains.
The network is taken from the European Environment Agency’s inventory of Nationally designated areas (NatDA, long known as the Common Database on Designated Areas, CDDA). This is the channel through which 38 Eionet countries report their protected areas to the World Database on Protected Areas, so Kosovo’s entry is its own official register rather than a third-party compilation.


237Designated sites


1,261 km²Protected network


11.6%Of the national territory


21,069Records inside a site


45%Of all records


2,262Species inside a site


21,069 of the 46,831 quality-checked records — 45 per cent — fall inside a designated site, and they carry 2,262 species between them. Against a network covering 11.6 per cent of the country that looks like a striking concentration, and it is worth taking apart before it is believed.
Most of it is one place. Ligatina e Hencit/ Radevës, a wetland of 1.10 km², supplies 13,346 of those records on its own — 63 per cent of everything inside the network, from 0.09 per cent of its area. Set that single site aside and 7,723 of the remaining 33,485 records fall in a protected area, 23 per cent against an 11.6 per cent share of the land.
Roughly twice the records per unit area, then, rather than five times — a real concentration, but a modest one, and it says as much about where people go to look as about what lives there. The section on survey coverage makes the same point in administrative units.

What the register contains






Kosovo’s register holds 237 designated sites, and it comes in two shapes. 48 carry a mapped boundary; the other 189 are recorded as a single point. That split is not a gap in the data — it is what the sites are. Every national park, strict nature reserve, protected landscape, nature park and wetland is a polygon. The point-only sites are all natural monuments, which in Kosovo means individual veteran trees, springs and caves, most of them smaller than a tenth of a hectare. A point is an honest way to record a stand of oak; a polygon would imply a precision the register does not claim.
A further 19 features are strict-protection zones — the strictly protected cores of sites the table already lists, not separate sites. They hold 762 records. Their area and their records are contained in the rows above rather than additional to them, which is why they are labelled as a role rather than counted as sites, and why the columns in that table must not be added up.


Which sites hold the evidence






Counted by site, the coverage looks thin: 28 of the 48 sites with a mapped boundary hold no quality-checked GBIF record at all. Counted by area, it looks the opposite — those 28 sites come to 4.17 km² between them, 0.3 per cent of the mapped network, and the remaining 99.7 per cent does have records.
Both readings are true, and the difference between them is the finding. The gaps are almost entirely in the small sites: 26 of the 28 are natural monuments, and the median one covers 0.017 km². Every national park, the nature park and the wetland are recorded in; it is the municipal-scale sites that are not.
The strict-protection zones are the sharper gap. These are the most tightly protected ground in the country, and 7 of the 19 hold no record — 12.3 km² of the 108.9 km² under strict protection, 11 per cent of it, with no openly published occurrence evidence behind it.
A site with no records is not a site with no species; it is a site nobody has surveyed, or one whose surveys were never published to GBIF. Which of the two it is, is worth knowing before the next field season is planned — and for the small municipal sites in particular, a single visit would produce the first open record either way.






WarningThree ways to misread this table





The IUCN column is not the Red List. It is the IUCN protected-area management category — Ia, Ib, II, III, V — which says how a site is run, not how likely anything in it is to go extinct. The Red List categories used elsewhere in this report are CR, EN, VU and so on. The two share an acronym and nothing else.
Records per square kilometre measure effort, not richness. The wetland at the top of that column carries more than twelve thousand records in barely a square kilometre, almost all of them bird observations submitted to one citizen-science platform from what is in practice one regularly watched spot. It is the same concentration described under survey coverage, seen through a different boundary. The species column is the more honest comparison.
The point-only sites hold no records here, and cannot. A point has no inside, so the 189 natural monuments recorded that way can never match a record by point-in-polygon, however well surveyed they are. They appear on the maps above, and in the published register, but they are absent from this table by construction rather than for want of evidence.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
section: Species protected under the EU Nature Directives
text:
Species protected under the EU Nature Directives
The annex lists were taken directly from the consolidated legal texts on EUR-Lex — 193 taxa on Birds Directive Annex I, and 1,333 across Habitats Directive Annexes II, IV and V — and every name was resolved against the GBIF backbone taxonomy so that records published under superseded names are still found. Larus minutus, for instance, is listed under that name but recorded as Hydrocoloeus minutus.
The table below shows the species of Community interest that have been recorded in Kosovo. The annexes are EU-wide lists dominated by Iberian, Alpine and Macaronesian endemics, so a listed species with no records here usually lies outside its natural range rather than indicating a survey gap; the meaningful gaps are the Balkan species one would expect to find and doesn’t.












WarningHow annex membership was determined





The species lists are built by R/build_directive_list.R, which parses the consolidated directives on EUR-Lex — the legally binding texts — rather than relying on a secondary checklist. Every name is then resolved against the GBIF backbone taxonomy, and occurrence records are selected by numeric key rather than by name, which is robust to synonymy and authorship variation.
Two details materially affect what appears in these subsets.
Rank matters when matching. A taxon listed at species rank is matched on both its species key and its taxon key, so records identified to subspecies are still captured. A taxon listed at subspecies rank is matched on that subspecies alone. Promoting subspecies listings to their whole species would be seriously misleading: the Birds Directive lists island endemics such as Columba palumbus azorica and Fringilla coelebs ombriosa, and matching those at species level would place every Wood Pigeon and Chaffinch in Kosovo on Annex I — around 1,450 records for subspecies confined to the Azores and the Canaries.
Exclusions are honoured. Where an annex lists a species except certain subspecies, as Annex V does for Rupicapra rupicapra, the excluded taxa are discarded rather than being read as listings in their own right.
Around 1.3 per cent of annex entries could not be resolved to a current GBIF taxon. These are names superseded since the directives were adopted, mostly Iberian and Macaronesian plants; none are species expected in Kosovo. The directive and annex columns are retained in every export so that any selection can be checked.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
section: Extinction risk: the IUCN Red List
text:
Extinction risk: the IUCN Red List
The EU annexes say what is legally protected. The IUCN Red List says what is at risk of extinction. The two overlap only partly, and a screening exercise needs both: a species can be at serious risk without appearing on any annex, and much of what is annexed is of least concern globally.
Every species in the dataset was matched to its global Red List assessment through the GBIF backbone taxonomy.


















NoteReading these assessments with care





Two cautions apply.
The assessment is global, not national. A species of least concern across Europe may be on the edge of its range and genuinely rare in Kosovo, and nothing in this table would show it. A national red list is the instrument for that question; this is a screen, not a substitute.
Backbone matching can misfire. The Red List category is attached through the GBIF backbone taxonomy, which occasionally links a name to an assessment of a different taxon. One record in this dataset is attributed to a species assessed as Extinct, which for a beetle collected in the Balkans is far more likely to be a taxonomic mismatch than a rediscovery. Treat a surprising category as a question to check rather than as a finding.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
section: Invasive alien species of Union concern
text:
Invasive alien species of Union concern
The directives and the Red List say what is at stake. Regulation (EU) No 1143/2014 deals with one of the things that puts it at risk: invasive alien species, introduced by people outside their natural range, that damage the ecosystems they spread into. Its core is the Union list — species that may not be imported, kept, bred, sold or released anywhere in the EU, for which Member States must run surveillance, report every new finding and act on it early, and manage populations that are already widespread.
The Regulation binds EU Member States. As with the Nature Directives elsewhere in this report, it is used here as the reference list against which the evidence is screened, not as a statement of what applies in Kosovo today.


114Species on the Union list


5Recorded in Kosovo


24Records


2Inside a designated site


20Across the border, not recorded here


Of the 114 species on the list, five have any quality-checked record in Kosovo, and they have 24 records between them. Twelve of the records date from 2015 or later, every one of them through iNaturalist.org and Pl@ntNet — citizen science, in other words, rather than survey. The other twelve either predate 2000 or carry no date; they come from Freshwater fishes of the Western Balkans, Small mammals of Yugoslavia 1992 atlas and Freshwater fishes of Serbia and Montenegro.
Read that as a statement about recording, not about the country. Tree of heaven, the most-recorded of the five, has eight records here and 406 across the four neighbouring countries, 242 of them in Serbia. Invasive species are what recorders walk past: the widespread ones are too familiar to note, and few surveys set out to find them. An absence from the table below is therefore no evidence that a species is absent from Kosovo — and for this list that is the expensive mistake to make, because a species caught early is the only kind that can still be eradicated.






Two of the records fall inside a designated site: muskrat in Ligatina e Hencit/ Radevës (2025) and stone moroko in Mali Pashtrik dhe Liqeni i Vërmices (1992). A record inside a protected area is the one a site manager needs to hear about first. Every record is in the explorer below, under the EU invasive species filter.

The watch list: across the border, not yet recorded here
The Regulation is built around early detection, and the species most likely to be found in Kosovo next are the ones already established next door. The table below lists every Union-list species with records in at least one neighbouring country and none in this extract, most widespread first.












NoteHow the Union list was built, and how the watch list was counted





The list is taken from the legal texts. R/build_ias_list.R reads the consolidated Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1141 and the four acts that amended it, and resolves every name against the GBIF backbone. The list holds 114 species. 111 apply today; the other 3 were listed with a deferred date — Castor canadensis from 7 August 2027, Celastrus orbiculatus from 2 August 2027, Neogale vison from 7 August 2027 — and are kept here, since a screen should catch them before the date rather than after it. The consolidated text on its own would have missed all three: a consolidated version carries only what already applies.
It agrees with the checklist published on GBIF, species for species. The Research Institute for Nature and Forest (INBO) publishes the Union list as a checklist dataset (doi:10.15468/97aucj), and unlike the per-annex Nature Directive checklists on GBIF, which leave out species beyond the region they were compiled for, it is complete. It supplies the English names in the tables. It is not the source, because its names are linked to the GBIF backbone less well than they are chosen: two of its species have no backbone link at all, one because a single accent (“Triadica sebífera”) defeats GBIF’s name parser, and one for the reason in the next paragraph.
One listed name does not exist in the GBIF backbone. The 2025 amendment lists the American mink as Neogale vison, the genus it was moved to in 2021. Asked for that name, GBIF’s matching service returns the genus Neogale, which it holds as a synonym of Mustela — a “higher rank” match, at 94 per cent confidence, and no error. Taken at face value, that would put every native weasel, stoat and polecat on the list of invasive species. The build refuses such matches rather than quietly promoting a species listing to a whole genus, and resolves the mink through its former name to Mustela vison, where the backbone holds it.
Three listings are below species rank — Vespa velutina nigrithorax, Procambarus fallax f. virginalis and Pueraria montana var. lobata — and each is matched on its whole species. That is the opposite of the rule for the Birds Directive’s island subspecies, and deliberately so: each of these is the form of its species that is established in Europe, and most records are identified to species only.
The watch list is a dated screening aid, not evidence of the same standard as the rest of this report. The counts come from the GBIF occurrence API with the download’s own quality filters, counted on 28 September 2026, and they are not covered by the DOI above. The neighbours are selected by their GADM boundaries, which draw Serbia without Kosovo, so no record inside Kosovo is counted as Serbian. A record across the border may be a planted tree, a pond turtle or a museum specimen; check the records on GBIF before treating any one of them as an established population.

Explore the records
The GBIF Viewer’s most useful idea is its filter panel: pick the conservation criteria that matter to you, and see what is left. That is reproduced here for the records of conservation interest — everything listed on an EU annex, assessed as threatened, or on the Union list of invasive alien species — with the filtering done in your own browser, so it costs nothing to host and keeps working for as long as this page does.
Filters combine: choosing a class and a Red List category shows records that satisfy both. Selections are shared between the map and the table.

Every species in the cleaned dataset, with the evidence behind it. Search by scientific or common name; each name links to its GBIF species page, where the full record set, images and taxonomic history can be inspected.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Who published these records
GBIF-mediated data is other people’s work. Every record in this report was collected, verified and published by one of the institutions below, and crediting them is a condition of use rather than a courtesy.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Download the data
All seven extracts are published as GeoPackage (.gpkg, ready for QGIS or ArcGIS, geometry included) and CSV (flat table with coordinate columns). The smaller extracts are also published as Excel workbooks. All are open formats requiring no proprietary software. Every extract carries the iasUnionConcern and iasAppliesFrom columns, so any of them can be screened for invasive species without the matching being run again.

title: Biodiversity of Kosovo
text:
Methods and reproducibility
The entire analysis is scripted and version-controlled. To reproduce it:

Install the R packages listed below.
Add your GBIF credentials to .Renviron (see the repository README.md).
Run Rscript pipeline.R to acquire, clean, enrich and export the data.
Run quarto render to rebuild this website.

pipeline.R records its GBIF download key, so re-running it re-uses the existing DOI rather than minting a new one. Delete data/gbif_download/download_key.txt to force a fresh extract. The vernacular name, Red List and dataset-registry lookups are cached under data/, so only the first run makes those requests; so are the neighbouring-country counts behind the invasive-species watch list, which is why that table states the day they were taken.
The two species lists are built from the legal texts, by Rscript R/build_directive_list.R for the Nature Directive annexes and Rscript R/build_ias_list.R for the Union list of invasive alien species. Both write a CSV that is kept in the repository, so neither needs running again until the legislation changes.

title: GIS and biodiversity data management
text: This page gathers the material from the six sessions Jonáš Gaigr of the Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic gave at the mission. Every presentation is here as slides to view in the browser and as a PDF handout to download, next to the GBIF data site that several of the sessions used as their worked example.

title: GIS and biodiversity data management
text:
The mission
The Expert Mission on Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and biodiversity data management was organised by TAIEX, the European Commission’s Technical Assistance and Information Exchange instrument, in co-operation with the Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Infrastructure (case ID ETT IND/EXP 82606). For three days, experts from the Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic and the Ministry of Environment of the Slovak Republic worked with the institutions that hold Kosovo’s* biodiversity data.
Its aim was practical: to show how GIS supports environmental management, biodiversity conservation and the implementation of the Birds and Habitats Directives. That covered spatial analysis, habitat mapping, satellite and remote sensing data, the monitoring of protected areas, assessing the conservation status of habitats and species, and identifying Natura 2000 sites. Alongside it, the mission set out to bring spatial data management in line with EU standards and to strengthen co-operation between the institutions that collect and use the data.

* This designation is without prejudice to positions on status, and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo declaration of independence.

title: Towards Natura 2000
text:
The Ministry put a set of questions to the expert team about moving from Kosovo’s present biodiversity data towards a Natura 2000 network. This page answers them as far as they fall within five sessions of the mission: spatial analysis, condition evaluation, GBIF data, field data collection and automated reporting. How sites are proposed, how Article 17 reporting works and how the institutions divide the work are the subject of the sessions by Karel Chobot and Martin Koška, and are not answered here. The numbering follows the Ministry’s list; question 7 lies outside these sessions.
Each answer gives the recommendation first, then what Kosovo’s own data show about it. Those figures are computed from the same GBIF extract, protected-area register and pipeline as the main report, so they move with it.

title: Towards Natura 2000
section: 1. Which data are good enough for which decision
text:
1. Which data are good enough for which decision
Treat fitness for use as a property of each record, computed by a written rule, in three tiers: national screening, candidate-site delineation and the Standard Data Form (SDF). A record moves up a tier by gaining precision, currency, documentation and validation, never because the decision it is wanted for is more important.










National screening
Candidate-site delineation
Standard Data Form




Spatial precision
Within the screening cell; 10 km atlas records for 10 km screening only
Points to 100 m or better; habitat polygons mapped at 1:10,000
As for delineation, and tied to a survey unit: plot, transect, polygon


Currency
Any date; records before 2000 flagged as historical
Observed within the last 12 years, two six-year reporting cycles
From a standardised survey, ideally within the current reporting cycle


Documentation
A citable source (dataset DOI or reference); name resolved against a taxonomic backbone
+ observer, date and method; a photograph or specimen for difficult taxa
+ survey protocol, effort, and counts with their units


Validation
Automated: coordinates, country, outliers, name matching
Verified by a named specialist for the taxonomic group
+ checked at site level, and given an SDF data-quality code: G, M, P or VP


Can support
Where to look; gap analysis; survey planning
Drawing and justifying a boundary
The population, area and assessment fields of the SDF



The values are proposals for national agreement, not established standards. Keep them as rows in a table rather than sentences in a guideline, so that moving a threshold is a one-line change anyone can review, and the tier of every record can be recomputed when it moves.
Two rules hold at every tier. A missing record is not evidence of absence; only surveys that record effort and non-detections can support one. And a name resolved by a backbone can still be the wrong taxon: synonymy in a global backbone can fold a Balkan endemic into a widespread species, or a domestic animal into its wild ancestor. A record whose name changed during matching is one for a specialist to look at.

What Kosovo’s data show












Records
All
Stated uncertainty ≤ 100 m
… and observed since 2014
… and observer named




All records
46,831
3,180
3,045
2,644 (5.6 %)


Birds Directive, Annex I
4,215

Habitats Directive, Annex II

By these rules, 5.6 % of GBIF records could support a boundary, and even those still need a specialist’s verification. No GBIF record reaches the SDF tier on its own: the extract carries neither a survey protocol nor a measure of effort, and that tier needs both.
The Annex I bird row shows why the tiers matter. 82 % of Kosovo’s Annex I bird records come from eBird, which publishes the checklist’s location without a stated uncertainty. For a stationary count at a wetland that point is close to the birds; for a travelling checklist they may be kilometres away. The rule cannot tell the two apart, so it places both at the screening tier until the effort fields are read from eBird’s own dataset (question 6).
For Natura 2000 purposes GBIF is a screening layer, and a good one: it says where the evidence is and where it is missing. The precision profile in the main report gives the full distribution.
Discussed in: GBIF data (Day 2), “How precisely are the records placed?”; Field data collection (Day 3), “What a form enforces at the point of capture”. A 15 m accuracy constraint on the device makes a new record delineation-grade at the moment it is captured.

title: Towards Natura 2000
section: 2. From the screening grid to a site boundary
text:
2. From the screening grid to a site boundary
The grid says where to look; the boundary comes from the ground. Use the 5 × 5 km cells to rank where evidence concentrates, then discard the cell edges entirely. Draw the candidate boundary from ecological and physical units at 1:10,000, and record the reason for each stretch of it.

Screen. Score the cells from screening-tier evidence: listed features, records, survey effort. Keep the evidence score and the effort count in separate columns, so that a cell that is merely well visited is not mistaken for one that is rich.
Form search areas. Merge adjacent priority cells and buffer them generously. This is an analysis envelope, never a draft boundary; from here on, cell edges play no part.
Assemble the ecological layers inside it. Annex I habitat polygons from field mapping (question 3); the habitat around delineation-grade species records, which means breeding and feeding areas and not just the point; catchments and a terrain model; Copernicus land-cover layers; roads and settlements as barriers.
Draw along those units. Use a habitat edge, a watershed, a forest-stand edge or a river. Snap the line to features visible on the orthophoto or the cadastre at 1:10,000, so that it can be found on the ground and in the land register.
Record why. Give every boundary segment a boundary_basis attribute: habitat edge, watershed, road, cadastral parcel, expert judgement. A boundary whose reasons are written down can be defended; one whose reasons are not will be reopened at every consultation.
Test it automatically. Flag any candidate whose boundary runs along grid lines for more than a small share of its length (10 % is a reasonable start). Flag any long straight segment that follows no mapped feature. A site shaped like its screening cells fails the test by construction.
Check what the line leaves out. Run the site evidence report on the candidate polygon and a 1 km ring around it. Records just outside a boundary are the best guide to what it has cut off.

Keep the grid for what it does well: screening, planning surveys and, later, the distribution maps of Article 17-style reporting. Store every record at its own precision and derive the grid from it, never the reverse. The one exception is an atlas record, whose true precision is the cell.

What Kosovo’s data show
Ligatina e Hencit/Radevës is the country’s richest site for Annex I birds, and its designated polygon covers 1.1 km². Inside it, GBIF holds 2,408 Annex I bird records of 43 species. Within 5 km outside it lie a further 633 records of 34 species, about 21 % of all the Annex I bird records in and around the site. 5 of those species were never recorded inside. The richest locality in that ring, “M9 Bridge over Sitnica River”, lies 2.2 km from the boundary and holds 25 Annex I species.
The birds use more of the landscape than the designated wetland. An SPA boundary copied from the national designation, or from a screening cell, would leave that out. The ring in step 7 is what shows it.
Discussed in: Spatial analysis (Day 1), “Fragmentation: connection, not just cover”; Automated reporting (Day 3), “A pilot, end to end”. Karel Chobot’s case study (Day 1) covers how the Czech sites were proposed.

title: Towards Natura 2000
section: 3. Mapping Annex I habitats before assessing them
text:
3. Mapping Annex I habitats before assessing them
Several Annex III criteria need both an area and a condition, and only a polygon map carries both. These include representativity, relative surface, and the degree of conservation of structure and function. Points, localities and centroids say where to map first; they cannot be summed into an area. Map in the field at 1:10,000, record condition as attributes scored by a written rule, and validate a random sample independently before any figure goes into an assessment.








Element
Recommended minimum
Czech practice, for comparison




Base and scale
Field mapping on a colour orthophoto, drawn at 1:10,000 (1:5,000 where detail requires)
Orthophoto at 1:10,000 or 1:5,000


Minimum mapping unit
About 0.25 ha for habitats that normally form large stands; smaller for rare or high-value stands
0.15–0.25 ha recommended for extensive types; smaller only for rarer or high-quality stands


Small and linear habitats
Springs, fens, small wetlands and caves as points or lines, with the true area or width recorded
Points and lines for occurrences under about 2,500 m² or narrower than 50 m, with true area or width recorded


Mosaics
One segment may hold several habitats, each with its share (%) and its own condition
Mosaic segments; more than five components referred to the methodologist


Boundary changes
Recorded when a boundary moves by more than about 30 m
About 30 m


Attributes per habitat
Annex I and national code; share of the segment; representativity; degradation; structure and function; typical species present; pressures; surveyor; date; photograph
Share and area per habitat; representativity, degradation, structure and function, regional context; surveyor and date per segment


Condition score
Derived from the attributes by a published lookup table, not judged afresh for each site
A quality lookup table, amended when a new combination occurs


Validation
Independent re-survey of a random 5–10 % of segments, reported as agreement on the habitat code and on the condition class
—



Czech practice follows the AOPK ČR methodology for updating the national habitat-mapping layer (Lustyk & Guth 2011). The recommended column is written for a first national map; a country mapping for the first time can hold to the same standard from the start and avoid retrofitting it.

Typical species from GBIF
Yes, to decide where to map first, but not for what is reported. The Interpretation Manual of European Union Habitats lists characteristic species for each Annex I type. Where several of them are recorded together in one 1 km cell, that cell is a candidate for early field mapping. The method works where the typical species are conspicuous and well recorded: aquatic and riparian types, and dry grasslands with their orchids and butterflies. It works poorly for forests defined by their dominant trees, and for habitats whose indicators are bryophytes or small sedges. It cannot give an area, a condition or an SDF figure. Co-occurrence is not a diagnosis either: most typical species also occur outside the habitat they characterise.
In Kosovo the plant record limits it further. Plants make up 8 % of GBIF records: 3,740 records of 938 species, of which 1,147 state an uncertainty of 100 m or better. 417 lie in Sharri National Park, which covers more than 500 km². Two or three habitat types chosen for well-recorded indicators are a fair test of the method; a national screen would mostly show where botanists have been.
Discussed in: Condition evaluation (Day 2), “A first habitat map: the minimum standard”; Field data collection (Day 3), “When the map is the working document” and “Where to start on Monday”. Karel Chobot’s habitat session (Day 1) covers monitoring design.

title: Towards Natura 2000
text:
4. Judging sufficiency without national totals
Do not wait for the denominator; make its uncertainty explicit. Estimate each national total as a range, compute the network’s share at both ends, and record a conclusion for every feature in the categories the EU’s own sufficiency process uses. Where the honest answer is that more research is needed, that process has a category for it.








Interim approach
How
Suits




The total as a range
Lower bound: the mapped or known area or population. Upper bound: modelled potential from land cover, terrain, geology and known records. Compute the network’s share against both.
Habitats with partial mapping


Occupied cells, allowing for effort
Share of occupied grid cells (the EEA 10 km grid) that fall in the network, counting only cells actually surveyed for that group
Species with scattered records


Representation across the range
Every main part of the range covered: massif, catchment, altitude belt
Every feature, whatever the data


All significant known localities
Where a feature is known from only a few sites, include every significant one
Rare and priority features


The neighbours’ figures
Article 17 estimates of neighbouring Member States and Emerald Network data of neighbouring Bern Convention Parties, as a check on plausibility
Transboundary features



The Commission’s working reference values are often quoted as a pass mark. A network holding more than 60 % of a feature’s resource is generally taken as sufficient, and one holding 20 % or less as a priority for scrutiny. They were designed as a pre-selection filter, and the current criteria say they “can never be used in isolation”. With a denominator given as a range, judge rare and priority features on the smaller of the two shares.
The conclusion codes of the EU sufficiency process are an honest way to record an interim result:







Code
Meaning




SUF
Sufficient: no further sites needed


IN MIN
Insufficient, minor: the feature should be added to the SDFs of sites already proposed


IN MOD
Insufficient, moderate: one or more further sites or extensions needed


IN MAJ
Insufficient, major: no site for the feature has been proposed yet


SR
Scientific reserve: further research needed to identify the most appropriate sites


SR Ref List
Scientific reserve on the reference list: regular occurrence still to be confirmed


CD
Correction of data: the SDF information needs correcting or completing



Keep one row per feature in a sufficiency ledger. Each row records the denominator range and its method, a data-quality code, the network’s share, the conclusion code, its date, and what evidence would change it. That last column turns every SR into a survey commission with a deadline, and makes the interim state as transparent as the final one.
Discussed in: Spatial analysis (Day 1), “A missing baseline is not a reason for inaction”. The biogeographical process itself is part of Karel Chobot’s sessions.

title: Towards Natura 2000
text:
5. Records that survive being shared
This page answers the data side of the question. Every record needs a permanent identifier, a traceable source, a version history and a validation status. Duplicates are linked, not deleted. Sensitivity is handled by generalising the public view, not by hiding the record. Ownership and the arrangement between the institutions are the subject of the joint database-architecture session (Day 1) and Martin Koška’s governance session (Day 2).







Element
Recommendation




Identifiers
A permanent UUID for every record, survey event and dataset, never re-used, with the provider’s own identifier kept alongside (Darwin Core occurrenceID). A site keeps its code through every boundary version.


Provenance
Dataset, source document, observer and method, stored as fields rather than a note.


Duplicates
Link, do not delete. Records of the same taxon, date and place from different sources share a cluster identifier; analyses count the cluster once and cite every source.


Versions
Every change to a record logged: who, when, what. Every analysis and every SDF submission made from a dated snapshot with its own DOI. Boundaries and SDFs released as numbered versions.


Validation
A status on every record, advanced in order: automated checks at import; the taxon specialist for the group; sign-off at site level; approval for SDF use.


Sensitive data
One store at full precision. The public view generalises listed sensitive species; named users under a data-use agreement see full precision, and access is logged. The sensitive list has an owner, a review cycle, and species can come off it.


Interoperability
Darwin Core for occurrences; INSPIRE Protected sites, Species distribution and Habitats and biotopes for services, through the national geoportal; one taxonomic backbone and shared code lists.



Duplication is already present in the published record. 77 groups of records, 163 records in all, describe the same species on the same day at the same place (to about 100 m) and were published in different datasets. Counted as they stand, they inflate the evidence; deleted, they lose a source. Linked, both counts are right. GBIF performs the same kind of linking across its whole index, and a national system can take its clusters as a starting point.
Discussed in: Spatial analysis (Day 1), “One central Biodiversity Information System” and “NDOP: open by default, precise by permission”.

title: Towards Natura 2000
section: 6. Bird data for Special Protection Areas
text:
6. Bird data for Special Protection Areas
Keep one table of bird records and derive the layers from it. Annex I species (Article 4(1)) and regularly occurring migratory species (Article 4(2)) belong in attributes, not in separate datasets that drift apart. To move from IBA, KBA and occurrence data to an SPA proposal, each species that is to qualify the site needs three things. It needs a current population estimate from standardised counts, and a stated criterion that estimate meets. It also needs a boundary drawn around the habitat the population actually uses.








Field
Content
Why




Annex I
Yes or no, from the consolidated Directive
The Article 4(1) trigger


Regular migrant
Yes or no, from a national list the Ministry adopts and versions
The Article 4(2) trigger; the list is a decision, not a lookup


Population type
p permanent, r reproducing, c concentration, w wintering: the SDF codes
One species can need different sites in different seasons


Breeding evidence
Possible, probable or confirmed, as in the European breeding bird atlas
A record in the breeding season is not a breeding record


Count and unit
A number, with its unit: pairs, individuals, males, calling males
Only counts with units can be summed or set against a threshold


Method and effort
Protocol, duration, distance, whether all species were reported
Turns a record into a survey, and makes absence usable



The working layers are views over that one table: Annex I breeding, Annex I passage and wintering, regular migrants, and congregations. When a record is corrected, every layer follows.
What an SPA proposal needs, beyond the IBA:

The IBA inventory is the starting point. The Court of Justice has treated it as the best available scientific reference for judging whether enough SPAs have been classified (Case C-3/96, Commission v Netherlands). An IBA is still not an SPA proposal: its boundary is often coarse, and some of its qualifying species cannot trigger an SPA at all (see below).
A population estimate for each trigger species, given as minimum and maximum with a unit, a year and an SDF data-quality code. It should come from standardised surveys over at least two or three seasons:

territory mapping or point counts for breeding birds;
nest surveys for raptors;
International Waterbird Census counts for wintering waterbirds;
standardised counts at passage bottlenecks.

The criterion it meets. BirdLife’s EU-level criteria are tested definitions: C2, the site regularly holds at least 1 % of a flyway or EU population of a species threatened in the EU; C6, the site is one of the five most important in its region for such a species.
A boundary around what the birds use: nesting, feeding and roosting areas, including the fields or river they commute to. Check it against the IBA outline; do not copy it.
eBird’s own dataset for analysis. Request the eBird Basic Dataset from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology. It carries the effort fields and whether each checklist reports every species detected, which turns a checklist’s missing species into non-detections. The copy on GBIF is presence-only.

The best bird site in the data is not an IBA
Ligatina e Hencit/Radevës holds 43 of the 70 Annex I bird species recorded in Kosovo. It is designated nationally as a wetland and appears in no IBA inventory. It is therefore the case for the occurrence-data route to an SPA, and it is where standardised counts are most obviously missing. Its birds also differ by season, which is the population-type field at work. 7 of its Annex I species were never recorded there in the breeding season: they are passage or wintering birds, and an SDF would list them as c or w.

title: Towards Natura 2000
text:
8. A pilot, end to end
Yes. Take two contrasting areas through the whole workflow in one field season before applying the method nationally: Sharri National Park for the habitat route and Ligatina e Hencit/Radevës for the bird route. A pilot tests the method, the data model and the division of work at a scale where mistakes are cheap. It also produces the first draft Standard Data Forms along the way.

Two draft SDFs and a lessons log



The lessons log is the main product. It records every step that took longer than planned, every attribute nobody could fill in, and every rule that had to change. The national method is revised from it before roll-out, which is the point of doing two sites first rather than two hundred.
The evidence packs for step 2 can be produced today, from data already in this repository:
Rscript site_reports.R --site NP_001 --site SAC_001
